clinicalPearls: A mature B-cell lymphoma of pre-germinal-centre origin defined by the translocation t(11;14) that juxtaposes CCND1 with the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus and overexpresses cyclin D1
The neoplastic cells are typically CD20-positive and CD5-positive with SOX11 expression, but unlike chronic lymphocytic leukaemia are CD23-negative
Often presents at an advanced stage in older adults with widespread lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, marrow and blood involvement, and sometimes gastrointestinal lymphomatous polyposis
The blastoid and pleomorphic variants are morphologically aggressive and carry a worse prognosis, especially with high proliferation index or TP53 abnormalities
A leukaemic non-nodal variant, often SOX11-negative, behaves more indolently and may be observed initially
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating cyclin D1 overexpression and/or t(11;14), with SOX11 useful in the rare cyclin D1-negative cases
Management uses chemoimmunotherapy incorporating anti-CD20 therapy, often with autologous HSCT in fit patients and BTK-inhibitor targeted agents in relapse
reference.pathophysiology: Mantle cell lymphoma arises from a mature B cell of the follicle mantle zone, generally before germinal-centre transit. The defining event is the t(11;14) translocation, which places the CCND1 gene under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer and leads to constitutive overexpression of cyclin D1, dysregulating the cell cycle at the G1-S transition. The transcription factor SOX11 is commonly expressed and contributes to the tumour phenotype. Additional genomic lesions affecting DNA-damage response and cell-cycle pathways, notably TP53 and CDKN2A alterations, drive more aggressive blastoid disease. The tumour disseminates widely, colonising the mantle zones of follicles and infiltrating nodes, spleen, marrow, blood and the gastrointestinal tract.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (for blastoid variant)
additionalInvestigations: Lymph node or tissue biopsy with immunohistochemistry showing cyclin D1 and SOX11 positivity
FISH or molecular testing to confirm t(11;14) CCND1-IGH
Flow cytometry demonstrating CD20-positive, CD5-positive, CD23-negative B cells
Assessment of proliferation index (Ki-67) for prognostic stratification
TP53 mutation and deletion analysis given its strong prognostic impact
PET-CT and bone marrow examination for staging, with gastrointestinal endoscopy where indicated
redFlags: Blastoid or pleomorphic morphology with high proliferation index indicating aggressive disease
TP53 abnormality predicting resistance to standard chemoimmunotherapy
Rapidly progressive bulky disease with B symptoms and rising lactate dehydrogenase
Central nervous system involvement in aggressive variants
Tumour lysis risk with high tumour burden at treatment initiation
reference.prognosis: Classic mantle cell lymphoma is generally incurable with a relapsing course, though modern chemoimmunotherapy, HSCT and targeted agents have improved survival; blastoid morphology, high Ki-67 and TP53 abnormalities predict poor outcomes, whereas the leukaemic non-nodal SOX11-negative variant can follow an indolent course.
pitfalls: Confusing the disease with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, both CD5-positive, without checking CD23 and cyclin D1
Missing the rare cyclin D1-negative variant, where SOX11 and t(11;14) alternatives aid diagnosis
Treating the indolent leukaemic non-nodal variant as aggressively as classic disease
Overlooking TP53 status, which should influence treatment choice
Failing to consider gastrointestinal involvement, which is common even when asymptomatic
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on mantle cell lymphoma
management: Treat fit patients with intensive induction chemoimmunotherapy combining an anti-CD20 antibody (rituximab) with a cytarabine-containing regimen, followed by autologous haematopoietic stem-cell transplant consolidation
Give rituximab maintenance to prolong remission after induction
Use a less intensive rituximab-bendamustine-based regimen for older or less fit patients
Employ Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as ibrutinib at relapse and increasingly earlier in the disease course
Adopt active surveillance for the indolent leukaemic non-nodal SOX11-negative variant
Recognise TP53-aberrant disease as chemo-resistant and prioritise novel agents, CAR-T therapy or clinical trials
Stage and monitor with PET-CT and bone marrow examination, managing tumour lysis risk during treatment
Coordinate through haemato-oncology, considering allogeneic transplant or CAR-T in refractory disease
